The rollout also highlights the broader trend of integrating PQC into existing security workflows rather than treating it as a separate, after‑the‑fact upgrade, though users should still monitor performance impacts and the evolving NIST standardization timeline.

Cloudflare has launched its Post-Quantum GeoKey Manager in closed beta, integrating NIST-standardized post-quantum cryptography to enforce strict geographical boundaries on customer private key access. item.title: Leiden University and Riverlane Research Reveals Distance-Losing Flaw in Correlated Decoding Below Threshold
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is important because it pinpoints a subtle but consequential flaw in correlated decoding that can erode the effective code distance and raise logical error rates even when operating below threshold—a problem that has lingered under the radar of many QEC implementations. By introducing a simple regularization parameter that restores the expected distance scaling without extra computational cost, the work offers an immediately applicable fix for surface‑code and other low‑density parity‑check decoders that are already being deployed on near‑term hardware. It also underscores how careful decoder design remains as critical as physical qubit improvements for achieving fault tolerance, reminding researchers to validate decoding assumptions against realistic noise models.

Leiden University and Riverlane research uncovered a flaw in correlated decoding, causing a loss of effective code distance and higher logical failure rates in quantum error correction. They introduced a new regularization parameter to fix this, restoring nominal distance scaling and improving accuracy without adding computational overhead. This discovery offers a crucial design principle for future quantum decoding architectures. Chalmers University of Technology has developed TRIO pulses, a new quantum control framework for superconducting processors. This breakthrough offers a way to reduce recalibration overheads in large-scale quantum processors and has been demonstrated with an X-gate achieving 99.90% fidelity. item.title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a full‑stack quantum workflow could tackle the notoriously hard problem of screening strongly correlated oxygen‑electrode materials for solid‑oxide fuel and electrolysis cells, moving beyond classical density‑functional tricks to quantum impurity solvers that deliver finite‑temperature Green’s functions. By embedding GW‑based methods such as GW+DMFT or SEET within a quantum simulation of the active space, the authors outline a concrete path toward quantum advantage in predicting vacancy formation energies and migration barriers—key metrics for electrolyte‑electrode performance. If the projected qubit counts and thermal‑state preparation costs can be met with near‑term error‑corrected hardware, the approach could dramatically shorten materials discovery cycles for high‑efficiency energy conversion devices.

We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

item.title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces StateDRIFT, a problem‑aware twist on the popular qDRIFT randomised simulation technique that tailors its sampling distribution using information about the initial state and observable of interest, thereby cutting both bias and variance. By solving a modest optimisation at each Trotter step, the authors demonstrate order‑of‑magnitude reductions in two‑qubit gate counts for realistic molecular dynamics (e.g., BeH₂ drops from ~11 k to under 1 k gates), a gain that could make high‑fidelity Hamiltonian simulation feasible on near‑term devices. The approach does rely on auxiliary classical estimates—via tensor‑network surrogates or classical shadows—but the reported savings suggest a practical pathway for integrating smarter sampling into quantum‑simulation pipelines.

Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that simply adding more qubits does not automatically yield better modal analyses; it rigorously refines the deflation condition for variational quantum eigensolvers and quantifies how approximate projectors and Pauli‑term growth limit accuracy in realistic finite‑element problems. By mapping a generalized eigenproblem to a mass‑orthonormal Hamiltonian via Cholesky whitening, the authors expose a concrete resource bottleneck—an order‑of‑magnitude increase in operator density—that explains why current VQE implementations still lag classical methods despite modest qubit counts. Amplitude encoding stores an N-degree-of-freedom structural mode using ceiling(log2 N) qubits. This article develops an evaluation framework for variational quantum eigensolvers in finite-element structural dynamics. A Cholesky transformation maps the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric mass-orthonormal Hamiltonian, ensuring Euclidean quantum-state orthogonality equals structural mass orthogonality. For higher modes, the deflation penalty condition is sharpened to a necessary-and-sufficient threshold, with a Davis-Kahan bound quantifying effects of approximate projectors. Numerical studies separate mapping correctness, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, finite-shot uncertainty, and damage localization. For 128-DOF chains, consistent-mass whitening increases transformed-operator density from 0.023 to 0.308 and Pauli terms from 576 to 2950. Exact state-vector experiments show qubit count and circuit expressibility are distinct. At 10^5 shots per Pauli term, first-mode frequency RMS error is 2.45%. item.title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that AI‑driven agents can automatically discover and certify quantum circuit optimizations, turning a traditionally manual, heuristic process into a reproducible, verifiable workflow. By integrating an exact verifier built through the same autonomous loop, the method achieves up to 73 % reductions in gate counts for key compilation tasks such as fermion‑to‑qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis—outperforming existing hand‑tuned and state‑of‑the‑art tools. Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the power of projected quantum kernels can stem from the physics of the feature map itself rather than from brute‑force classical hyperparameter sweeps, highlighting a genuine quantum advantage in kernel design. Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. However, recent PQK studies often rely heavily on extensive classical hyperparameter tuning of the radial basis function (RBF) kernel parameter and the support vector machine regularization parameter. The extensive tuning can mask the true representational power of the underlying PQKs induced by quantum feature maps, which has not been explored in detail. Thus, this work aims to expose the structural capabilities of PQKs by isolating and evaluating their native inductive bias through comparisons between untuned and tuned PQKs against the RBF baseline. Furthermore, we propose novel quantum feature maps that leverage two-qubit entanglement to capture multivariate correlations in IoT data. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. This reveals that superior quantum architectural design can yield structurally better PQKs with improvements arising from quantum-mechanical properties rather than from classical hyperparameter tuning.

item.title: Fluctuation-free Quantum Battery Charging Enabled by Bell-like Entangled and Separable Charger States
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by carefully tailoring the quantum state of a charger—using specific Bell‑like entangled or separable configurations—it is possible to eliminate shot‑to‑shot energy fluctuations when charging a three‑qubit quantum battery, turning intrinsic quantum randomness from a bug into a design feature. The implication of entanglement in quantum battery charging remains poorly understood. In addition, intrinsic quantum randomness poses a fundamental challenge to charging uniformity across distinct trials. To address these issues, we study a three-qubit system within a cascaded collision frame, with two qubits acting as the charger and the third serving as the battery. After each collision, an adaptive measurement is performed on the charger, yielding four conditional post-measurement battery states with identical expected stored energy. For arbitrary fixed charger states, we derive analytical expressions for the recurrence relation of stored energy. We find that stored-energy fluctuations depend on whether the dynamics relies on the battery phase \(γ_n\). For two Bell-like families of entangled states, together with their computational basis states termed Bell-like separable states, the dynamics is \(γ_n\)-independent and fluctuations vanish, whereas for other entangled and separable states, fluctuations emerge. These insights establish a paradigm for engineering charger states to design uniform-charging quantum-battery architectures despite inherent quantum randomness.

item.title: Noise redistribution by stabilizer codes: an organizing view of concatenated three-qubit codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a clean “noise‑redistribution” picture that shows how any stabilizer code automatically reshapes an incoming error channel into a block‑diagonal logical map, eliminating the need for artificial Pauli twirling and making the effect of each concatenation step analytically tractable. By applying the framework to the simplest three‑qubit bit‑flip and phase‑flip codes, the authors derive a concrete threshold (γ ≈ 0.30) for amplitude‑damping noise that rivals the performance of the more complex five‑qubit code, suggesting a practical route to low‑overhead error correction on near‑term devices. The work also points toward adaptive concatenation schemes that could exploit dominant logical errors in real time, although its ideal‑recovery assumptions mean experimental validation under realistic gate imperfections will be essential.

We present an organizing framework for concatenated quantum error correction based on the observation that the syndrome projection of a stabilizer code reshapes the noise channel in a code-determined manner. For any stabilizer code, one level of QEC maps the physical noise to a block-diagonal logical channel whose diagonal Pauli weights are fixed by the code geometry. Coherences between different syndrome classes vanish, and no physical Pauli twirl is required to reach this block-diagonal form. Concatenation can then be viewed as the iteration of the same redistribution step: the dominant logical error after one level selects the code used at the next. We instantiate the framework with the two smallest stabilizer codes, the bit-flip and phase-flip codes, and apply it to amplitude damping. The redistribution rules give the concatenation protocol $C_2(\hatσ_y) C_1(\hatσ_x)$, whose ideal-recovery fidelity scales as $f_l=1-\mathcal O(γ^2)$. Solving the crossover condition $F_l>F_{l-1}$ in the ideal-gate limit yields a critical damping parameter $γ_c\approx0.30$; in terms of the initial channel fidelity, $f=1-1.72755γ^2$. Under the same ideal-recovery assumption, we compare the overall gate accuracy rate with that of the five-qubit code. The scope of the framework, in particular for coherent and correlated noise, is stated explicitly.

item.description:

Lattice-surgery compilation places logical qubits on a grid of surface-code tiles and routes their interactions. Sparse static layouts limit routing contention but reserve space that often remains idle. Reducing this reservation requires balancing area savings against additional gate serialization and qubit movement. In this paper, we present a co-designed dynamic architecture and compiler that allocates routing space according to circuit demand. The architecture preserves a fixed virtual qubit floorplan while allowing its physical spacing to change between execution stages. The compiler coordinates placement, scheduling, and routing to implement lattice surgeries using fewer physical qubits. Across our application benchmarks, our method reduces space-time volume by 55.6% in geometric mean and compiles 75.5 times faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration. A circuit-synthesis case study shows how our compiler exposes optimization tradeoffs.

item.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. II. System-parameter uncertainties and overall errors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that high‑fidelity CZ gates between tunable transmons can be made robust to realistic uncertainties in coupling strengths, anharmonicities and qubit frequencies, pushing gate errors below the 10⁻³ threshold even when parameters drift by several megahertz. By integrating optimal‑control techniques with dynamical decoupling and a symmetric‑detuning operating point, the authors show a practical route to reduce calibration overhead and improve reliability across successive hardware generations—a key step toward scalable superconducting error‑corrected processors. The results complement recent advances in fast, low‑leakage two‑qubit gates, though they still rely on coherence times that match today’s best transmon devices.

In the companion paper (Part I), we developed an optimal-control framework to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors in controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons. Here, we extend this framework to incorporate uncertainties in coupling strength, anharmonicities, and zero-flux qubit frequencies, enabling the design of high-fidelity gates robust against noise and parameter uncertainties. We classify these uncertainties by whether they perturb the off-diagonal coupling strengths or the diagonal detunings of the Hamiltonian, and we identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated through dynamical decoupling induced by strong detuning modulation. For a 30-ns gate, this strategy reduces the coupling error to $6.21\times10^{-7}$ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to $2π\times4$ MHz while keeping total gate infidelity below $10^{-3}$. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances the two dominant leakage-mediated interactions. A 24-ns gate operated near this point tolerates individual uncertainties of up to $2π\times5$ MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. We further optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance. The resulting stage-specific controls achieve lower infidelity and greater robustness. Together with the companion study (Part I), this framework offers a practical approach to balance speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

item.title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first time a full QKD security proof—specifically for BB84 with finite‑key composability—has been mechanically verified in Coq, closing a long‑standing gap between elegant theory and rigorously checked implementation. By reconstructing the smooth‑entropy framework, entropic uncertainty relation and Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma from first principles, FVQKD not only uncovers hidden side conditions that escaped earlier pen‑and‑paper arguments but also provides reusable formal infrastructure for future quantum‑cryptographic protocols. The result gives industry and standards bodies a stronger assurance that the unconditional security promised by QKD rests on provably sound mathematics, though scaling the approach to more complex or device‑independent schemes will still require substantial effort.

Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.

item.title: On the Structure of Quantum Finite-Level Systems: Decoherence-Free Subsystems, Quantum Nondemolition Variables, and Back-Action-Evading Measurements
item.description:

By formalising real coordinate transformations that preserve commutation relations and introducing “strongly aligned” subspaces, the authors provide tools that can be applied to design noise‑resilient logical qubits and ultra‑low‑noise sensors—capabilities that recent experiments on superconducting and trapped‑ion platforms are racing to exploit. The purpose of this paper is to conduct a comprehensive structural analysis of quantum finite-level systems in the Heisenberg picture, where the evolution of system observables is modeled by bilinear quantum stochastic differential equations (QSDEs). Firstly, real coordinate transformations that preserve commutation and anticommutation relations are characterized, and relative admissibility between different orthonormal Hermitian bases is formulated. Secondly, strongly aligned subspaces are introduced, based on which decoherence-free subsystems (DFSs) are constructed in general orthonormal Hermitian basis as well as the generalized Gell-Mann basis. Thirdly, conditions for the existence of quantum nondemolition (QND) variables are given in terms of both linear systems theory and spectral separation by output-signal observables. Finally, a sufficient condition for quantum back-action-evading (BAE) measurements is established. A four-qubit nearest-neighbor Heisenberg chain with collective dephasing illustrates these structural properties of quantum finite-level systems.

item.title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that universal fault‑tolerant computation can be achieved with a “just‑inject” strategy on high‑rate, concatenated self‑dual CSS codes, sidestepping the heavy lattice overhead of surface‑code magic‑state factories. By preparing and consuming multi‑qubit stabilizer and global |H⟩ states in parallel, the authors demonstrate an order‑of‑magnitude spacetime saving for the same T‑depth compared with conventional surface‑code approaches—a result that directly tackles one of the biggest bottlenecks in scaling quantum algorithms. We propose a quantum architecture that achieves addressable and parallel universal fault-tolerant logical in high-rate codes. The codes are obtained from the flexible concatenation of small-distance high-rate self-dual CSS codes. Addressable and parallel universal logic on the resulting $K$ logical qubits is injected by fault-tolerantly preparing and then consuming diverse logical $K$-qubit CSS stabilizer states and logical $\lvert H \rangle^{\otimes K}$ global magic states. Flag-at-origin is used to prepare the stabilizer resource states while a concatenated cultivation protocol prepares the global magic states. These resource states are consumed by Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets, which simultaneously perform quantum error correction. Any quantum algorithm with $T$-depth $D_T$ can be executed by consuming $12D_T$ or fewer resource states. We benchmark the fault-tolerant preparation of the resource states for several two-level concatenations of the $[[k+4,k,2]]$ H codes and the Hamming $[[15,7,3]]$ code. In particular, we find that the concatenated cultivation offers at least one order of magnitude spacetime reduction compared to cultivation in the surface code.

item.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that controlled‑Z gates on tunable transmons can be pushed to the physical speed limit—12 ns—with intrinsic error rates as low as 2×10⁻⁵, a fidelity level that meets the thresholds required for surface‑code fault tolerance. By integrating realistic dephasing models and identifying sweet‑spot operating points, the authors show how optimal‑control pulses can simultaneously deliver ultra‑fast gates and robustness against both fast electronic noise and slow 1/f flux fluctuations, addressing a key scalability bottleneck as calibration budgets shrink in larger processors. The framework also highlights transmon asymmetry as a practical design knob, suggesting that near‑term hardware upgrades could adopt these techniques without major architectural changes, though experimental validation of the predicted decoherence suppression will be essential.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

item.description:

By tightening the lower bound to match Raz’s upper bound and removing earlier technical restrictions, the work sharpens our understanding of where quantum information truly outperforms classical schemes in high‑dimensional geometry. The result not only advances communication‑complexity theory but also provides a concrete benchmark for future hardware demonstrations of quantum advantage in distributed computing tasks.

We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $Θ(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $Ω(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.

item.title: An entanglement band structure for general multiqubit states
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article extends the classic Majorana representation into a full “entanglement band structure,” showing that the reduced state of any qubit in an arbitrary multiqubit wavefunction sweeps out eigenvalue bands on the Bloch sphere and even exhibits non‑Hermitian exceptional points without any gain or loss. By mapping entanglement invariants to a Riemann‑surface‑like topology, the work provides a new geometric language for classifying multipartite entanglement that could streamline benchmarking of noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices where state tomography is costly. The five‑qubit result—pinning down an entanglement class up to only finitely many possibilities—suggests a practical route toward compact, hardware‑agnostic descriptors for complex quantum states, though experimental extraction of the band data remains an open challenge.

Majorana drew a symmetric multiqubit state as points on the Bloch sphere, antipodal to the zeros of its overlap with spin coherent states. Projecting only one qubit of a general state leaves the others in a state that varies with direction. Its entanglement invariants are eigenvalues of a non-Hermitian matrix and form bands over the sphere. Exceptional points appear, without gain or loss, where the entanglement family of the rest changes. Circling one exchanges two bands, so the bands form one Riemann surface. At five qubits it fixes the entanglement class up to finitely many choices.

item.title: Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first meter‑scale superconducting interconnects that can reliably shuttle quantum states between two 120‑qubit processors with ≈99 % fidelity and execute cross‑module CZ gates above 94 %, a performance level previously seen only in on‑chip couplings. By using indium pressure bonds and coaxial links that run perpendicular to the chip, the work shows a scalable hardware approach that could support dozens of parallel connections—a key requirement for modular quantum architectures competing with photonic or microwave‑bus schemes. The results suggest that large‑scale, distributed superconducting processors are now within experimental reach, although integrating error‑corrected logical qubits will still demand further improvements in gate fidelity and crosstalk management.

Modular quantum architecture requires long-distance quantum interconnects to stitch together individual processor modules. Such interconnects, long-distance couplers or L-couplers, must support coherent quantum operation over meter-scale distances and scale to multiple connections between any two modules. Here we demonstrate four L-couplers operating between two 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting qubit processors. Each L-coupler joins two Nighthawk lattice qubits through two frequency-tunable L-qubits, two RF-SQUID based "i2m" couplers, and 80 cm of superconducting aluminum coax. Each cable installs perpendicular to the processor surface, to enable denser connections, and is joined to the chip by an indium-to-indium room temperature pressure bond made after both modules were mounted. L-coupler modes near 5 GHz, with internal quality factors of 0.86 to 1.09e6, carry relay-based state transfer at a mean network benchmarking fidelity of 99.00%, with a best link of 99.29 +/- 0.07%. We then realize distant CZ gates between lattice qubits in separate modules at a mean fidelity of 94.75%, with a best link of 96.42 +/- 0.28%, and use them to generate entangled states across the two processors, including a demonstration of simultaneous Bell pair generation using two adjacent L-couplers. These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing.

item.title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers one of the first systematic measurements of how entanglement and coherence evolve inside leading variational optimizers, using a Bures‑metric framework that avoids full tomography. By showing that QAOA concentrates a large entanglement burst in its early layers while FALQON keeps resources modest, it gives designers concrete guidance on which algorithm may be more viable for near‑term hardware with limited coherence times. The findings also tie into the broader push to quantify and minimize quantum resource overheads, although they are based on a single Minimum Vertex Cover instance and will need scaling studies before general conclusions can be drawn.

Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are promising approaches for solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, the role played by quantum resources such as entanglement and coherence during the optimization process remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the evolution of these resources in two VQAs--the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON)--applied to the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. We employ a variational resource-quantification framework based on the Bures metric and Uhlmann's theorem, in which an auxiliary quantum circuit is optimized to identify the closest resource-free states. This approach allows us to quantify Bures entanglement and Bures coherence of the algorithmic states without requiring full quantum state tomography. For the considered problem instance, QAOA exhibits a pronounced accumulation of entanglement in its initial layers, followed by a progressive reduction as the algorithm converges toward the optimal solution. Its coherence likewise decreases overall with increasing circuit depth, although a finite residual value persists due to the degeneracy of the optimal-solution subspace. In contrast, FALQON exhibits a substantially lower entanglement peak, reached at larger circuit depth, followed by a decay as convergence proceeds. Its coherence decreases smoothly and monotonically together with the optimization error. These results reveal distinct quantum-resource trajectories associated with the two optimization strategies and illustrate how entanglement and coherence evolve as variational quantum states approach solutions of a classical combinatorial optimization problem.

By linking cloud‑scale data pipelines with noisy intermediate‑scale devices, firms can already offload specific optimization or simulation tasks and gather operational experience that will accelerate adoption once error‑corrected hardware arrives. The piece also cautions that without robust orchestration, software tooling, and security frameworks, early adopters risk falling behind the next wave of fully integrated quantum solutions.
